title: When recursion never stops
summary: What StackOverflowError means and how to fix it.

say.never: This version forgot to stop. With no base case, `triangle(3)` calls `triangle(2)`, then `triangle(1)`, then 0, then -1, and so on forever. Each call waits in memory for the next, until Java runs out of room and stops with a **StackOverflowError**.
say.bit: No base case means endless calls and a StackOverflowError.

steps.title: In your lesson: No way out

say.never: This version forgot to stop. With no base case, `factorial(3)` calls `factorial(2)`, then `factorial(1)`, then 0, then -1, then -2, and so on forever. Each call waits in memory for the next, until Java runs out of room and stops with a **StackOverflowError**.
say.bit: This version forgot to stop at 0, so it keeps calling `factorial(-1)`, `factorial(-2)`... forever.

board.caption: Exception: java.lang.StackOverflowError

say.never: The fix has two rules. Every path must reach a base case, so there's a place to stop. And every call must move *toward* it, so you actually get there. Here, `rows - 1` moves toward 1, and `rows <= 1` is where it stops.
say.bit: Every path needs a base case, and each call must move toward it.

say.never: The fix has two rules. Every path must reach a base case, so there's a place to stop. And every call must move *toward* it, so you actually get there. Here, `n - 1` moves toward 1, and `n <= 1` is where it stops.

say.never: Strings work the same way. A method that counts letters can shrink the text on every call: count one letter, then ask the same method about everything after it. When the text is empty, there's nothing left to count, and that's the base case.
say.bit: Strings recurse by shrinking the text each call; the empty string is the base case.
